stories.title: Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
stories.summary: The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people on board, when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Image source, International Organization for Migration Image caption, IOM workers receiving migrants near Guhere, north of the port town of Obock By Hafsa Khalil Published 11 October 2026, 13:05 BST Updated 5 hours ago At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said. The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says. The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered. "This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nl7M Finland's policymakers will spend the winter deciding where the ax should fall Image: Ardan Fuessmann/IMAGO Advertisement There's an uneasy mood in Finland , the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years. With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts. Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression. Finland's debt ratio climbed sharply since the COVID-19 pandemic Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%. Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine .

It caused extensive damage along the west of the island in the towns of Marsala and Petrosino, south of the city of Trapani. Dozens of people were reportedly injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily Continue reading...

stories.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protest
stories.summary: Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi. Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations

stories.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
stories.summary: Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

stories.title: Schools crisis in France: Investment fails to inspire confidence
stories.summary: For weeks, schoolchildren in France have been protesting the failing education system. Compared to many other countries, France invests heavily in education but critics say that the funds are not distributed fairly.
